statement: In Chinese men and in people of European descent, genetically higher alcohol intake compared with genetically lower intake is associated with higher blood pressure and with more high blood pressure (hypertension), and in the Chinese study the rise for each gram was about the same as with self-reported drinking; no paper read gives the absolute risk of hypertension by amount drunk. In 161,498 genotyped Chinese adults, men's systolic blood pressure was 4.3 mm Hg higher (95% CI 3.7 to 4.9) per 280 g of ethanol a week (40 g a day) of genotype-predicted mean intake, which, if the rise is even, is about 1.5 mm Hg per 100 g a week (editors' calculation), against 4.8 mm Hg (4.5 to 5.1) per 280 g a week of self-reported usual intake among men who drank; in women, few of whom drink, the same genotypes went with 0.6 mm Hg lower pressure (−1.0 to −0.1) (Millwood et al., 2019). In 56 European-descent studies, carriers of the ADH1B variant, who reported 17% less drinking, had systolic pressure 0.88 mm Hg lower (0.56 to 1.19 lower) and odds of hypertension of 0.94 (0.91 to 0.98; 104,570 people with hypertension), but the lower pressure was as large in people who said they did not drink (0.80 mm Hg lower) as in people who drank lightly to moderately (0.68 lower), which points either to misreported drinking or to a path other than current drinking (Holmes et al., 2014). In UK Biobank, a genetic score for alcohol use disorder was associated with hypertension, odds ratio 1.28 (1.18 to 1.39) per standard deviation of genetically predicted intake (Biddinger et al., 2022), and in European summary data genetically predicted drinking went with higher systolic and diastolic pressure, in units the paper's figure does not make clear (Larsson et al., 2020). In UK Biobank's self-reported data, the lower hypertension risk of people who drank moderately, against people who did not drink, was no longer statistically clear once six lifestyle factors were allowed for. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In a Chinese study, men's top blood-pressure number rose by about 4 points (mm Hg) for each extra 40 grams of alcohol a day that their genes predicted, about the same as when men were asked how much they drank. In European studies, people with a gene that makes them drink a little less had slightly lower blood pressure and less high blood pressure, and a gene score for alcohol problems went with more high blood pressure. The European gene also went with lower blood pressure in people who said they did not drink, so it may act in other ways too. The studies do not say how many more people out of 100 get high blood pressure at each amount.
population: Men in the China Kadoorie Biobank (161,498 genotyped adults; women as a check); people of European descent in 56 pooled studies (Holmes et al.), UK Biobank (Biddinger et al.; Mass General Brigham Biobank for replication) and UK Biobank-based summary data (Larsson et al.)
exposure: Genetically predicted alcohol intake (ALDH2 and ADH1B genotypes with area; the ADH1B rs1229984 variant; a 5-variant score for alcohol use disorder; up to 94 variants for log drinks a week), and self-reported usual intake among men who drank (China)
comparator: Lower genetically predicted intake (per 280 g/week of genotype-predicted mean male intake; non-carriers; per standard deviation); people who did not drink, for the conventional UK Biobank comparison
outcome: Systolic and diastolic blood pressure (mm Hg) and hypertension
magnitude: Millwood et al. 2019 (men; per 280 g/week, which is 40 g/day): systolic blood pressure +4.3 mm Hg (3.7–4.9) genetic, +4.8 (4.5–5.1) conventional among current drinkers; about +1.5 mm Hg per 100 g/week if linear (editors' calculation); women −0.6 (−1.0 to −0.1). Holmes et al. 2014 (intake-lowering ADH1B variant; 17.2% fewer units a week): systolic −0.88 mm Hg (−1.19 to −0.56), hypertension OR 0.94 (0.91–0.98); by self-reported drinking −0.80 (none), −0.68 (more than 0 to under 21 units/week), −1.70 (21 or more). Biddinger et al. 2022 (OR per SD of genetically predicted intake): hypertension 1.28 (1.18–1.39); within categories per 1 drink/day of allele score 1.3 (light), 1.7 (moderate), 2.6 (highest); conventional moderate-intake difference not significant after six lifestyle factors. Larsson et al. 2020: systolic 0.12 (0.05–0.20) and diastolic 0.15 (0.05–0.25) per SD of log drinks/week, units unclear. No absolute risks of hypertension by intake.

evidence.extracted: Men: systolic blood pressure rose 4.8 mm Hg (95% CI 4.5 to 5.1) per 280 g a week of usual self-reported intake among current drinkers (193,003 men) and 4.3 mm Hg (3.7 to 4.9) per 280 g a week of genotype-predicted mean intake (55,897 men in Figure 3, 55,879 in Table 2); HDL cholesterol rose 0.19 and 0.16 mmol/L and γ-glutamyltransferase 62 and 44 IU/L in the conventional and genetic analyses respectively.

The lower hazards of hypertension and coronary artery disease at moderate intake lost statistical significance after adjustment for smoking, body mass index, physical activity, cooked vegetable intake, red meat intake and self-rated health. The figure prints no values; read approximately by the first reader, the light-intake association was attenuated but not removed.

risk_of_bias.note: The genetic design protects against confounding by lifestyle and against illness changing drinking. In China the check in women showed a small path outside drinking in the opposite direction (−0.6 mm Hg), which would hide rather than create the rise in men, and the genetic and self-reported slopes agree. The ADH1B study's association in people reporting no drinking is a pleiotropy signal for that variant, and the UK Biobank score may act on other behaviours; because the largest study's two approaches agree and every study points the same way, not rated down (logged for the senior author under the round's rule).

inconsistency.note: All four studies point the same way.

indirectness.note: Blood pressure measured once at baseline in China; hypertension from records in the European data; the European estimates are per SD or per variant and cannot be put into grams. Stated, not rated.

dose_response.note: Not upgraded: the Chinese slope is a single estimate, and the within-category estimates in UK Biobank compare people grouped by reported drinking, which the score itself changes.

grade.reasoning: Mendelian randomization is observational and starts low (round brief). The design addresses confounding by lifestyle and reverse causation, and in the largest study genetic and conventional estimates agree while the check in women points the other way, so the editors do not rate down for confounding; pleiotropy remains possible for the ADH1B variant and for scores built on alcohol use disorder, and the design cannot show the curve at low intake. Low. Status replicated: three genetic studies in two ancestries (Millwood et al.; Holmes et al.; Biddinger et al.) point the same way, with Larsson et al. in the same direction but overlapping Biddinger et al.'s UK Biobank data and with unclear units; Holmes et al. and Millwood et al. share two authors.
